explanation.short: r6c6, r7c6, r9c6 ≠ 3: X-Wing on 3 (row 5 and row 8 / column 6 and column 8)
explanation.teach: Follow the 3s in row 5 and row 8: each has exactly two spots (row 5: r5c6 or r5c8; row 8: r8c6 or r8c8), and those spots line up in column 6 and column 8. The two 3s must sit on opposite corners of the rectangle, so they use up column 6 and column 8's 3s -- r6c6, r7c6 and r9c6 can't be 3. X-Wings show up when a digit has only two places in two parallel lines.

explanation.notation: Innies & outies as a virtual cage: 1 in r7c456,r9c4 => r7c45<>1
explanation.short: r7c4, r7c5 ≠ 1: rule of 45 -- the innie cells of box 8 total 14
explanation.teach: Box 8 must total 45. The cages lying completely inside add up to 14 + 9 = 23, so the uncovered cells r7c4, r7c5, r7c6 and r9c4 must total 45 - 23 = 22 (r9c4 is already 8, leaving 14 for the rest). Treat r7c4, r7c5 and r7c6 as a virtual cage of 14: the only fillings left are 3+4+7 or 1+6+7. A 1 in r7c4 or r7c5 leaves 13 for the other cells, but they can make at most 11. Rule-of-45 sums turn any nearly-covered house into an extra cage.

explanation.notation: Line / dot read without notes: r4c5=1
explanation.short: r4c5 = 1: every other digit is excluded, with a little reasoning in your head

Now use the rules in your head: 2 fails because its V (sum 5) partner r4c4 can only be 2, 4, 6, 7 or 9 at this point, and none of those allows a 2; 4 fails because its V (sum 5) partner r4c4 can only be 2, 4, 6, 7 or 9 at this point, and none of those allows a 4; 6 fails because its V (sum 5) partner r4c4 can only be 2, 4, 6, 7 or 9 at this point, and none of those allows a 6; 7 fails because its V (sum 5) partner r4c4 can only be 2, 4, 6, 7 or 9 at this point, and none of those allows a 7; 9 fails because its V (sum 5) partner r4c4 can only be 2, 4, 6, 7 or 9 at this point, and none of those allows a 9. Only 1 survives -- no pencil marks needed.

explanation.teach: Spot the pair: r5c4 {8,9}, r8c4 {8,9} in column 4. However they are arranged, 8 and 9 are used up there, which removes them from r1c4, r2c4, r6c4 and r7c4.

explanation.short: r2c5 = 8: the only 8 left in the notes of row 2
explanation.teach: In row 2, 8 has been squeezed down to a single cell, r2c5. A hidden single in the notes is easy to miss because the cell still shows several candidates -- scan one digit at a time across a house.

explanation.notation: Two rules together: in r6c6,r7c4567,r89c456 => r7c56<>9
explanation.short: r7c5, r7c6 ≠ 9: two rules together
explanation.teach: Take two rules together: list the digit combinations that satisfy both at once over their 11 open cells (digits that see each other differ, a house still needs its missing digits). Some candidates appear in none of them. So r7c5 cannot be 9 and r7c6 cannot be 9.

explanation.notation: Locked Candidates Type 1 (Pointing): 9 in b8 => r8c7<>9
explanation.short: r8c7 ≠ 9: pointing -- the 9s of box 8 are locked into row 8
explanation.teach: In box 8 the 9 can only go in r8c4, r8c5 or r8c6, which all lie in row 8. So box 8's 9 is also row 8's 9, and nothing else in row 8 can be 9: remove it from r8c7. Look for boxes where a digit's notes line up in a single row or column.

explanation.teach: In row 8, the cells r8c4 {8,9}, r8c6 {8,9} use only the digits 8 and 9 between them. 2 cells, 2 digits: those digits must fill exactly those cells, so no other cell of row 8 can have them -- clear them from r8c5.

explanation.short: r7c7 ≠ 9: Turbot Fish -- either r7c2 is 9 or r8c6 is 9
explanation.teach: Start from the idea that r7c2 is NOT 9: so r9c2 is 9 (the only other 9 in column 2), which stops r8c4 being 9, so r8c6 is 9 (the only other 9 in row 8). So at least one end is true: r7c2 is 9 or r8c6 is 9. Cell r7c7 sees both ends, so it can't be 9. This shape is a Turbot fish: a four-cell single-digit chain (strong-weak-strong). Single-digit chains like this are found by following one digit's conjugate pairs.

explanation.teach: Row 5 can only place its 3 in r5c5 or r5c6 -- all in box 5. That 3 is therefore box 5's 3 as well, which clears 3 from r4c4, r4c5 and r4c6.

explanation.notation: Innies & outies over several houses: 4 in r7c79,r8c7,r9c78 => r9c8<>4
explanation.short: r9c8 ≠ 4: rule of 45 -- the innie cells of box 9 total 7
explanation.teach: Box 9 must total 45. The cages lying completely inside add up to 7 + 7 = 14, so the uncovered cells r7c7, r7c9, r8c7, r9c7 and r9c8 must total 45 - 14 = 31 (r7c7 is already 7, r7c9 is already 8, r9c7 is already 9, leaving 7 for the rest). Treat r8c7 and r9c8 as a virtual cage of 7: the only fillings left are 1+6, 3+4 or 2+5. A 4 in r9c8 would need a 3 in r8c7, which isn't among its notes {1,4,5}. Rule-of-45 sums turn any nearly-covered house into an extra cage.

explanation.notation: Locked Candidates Type 2 (Claiming): 4 in row8 => r8c5<>4
explanation.short: r8c5 ≠ 4: claiming -- the 4 of row 9 is confined to box 8
explanation.teach: Row 9 can only place its 4 in r9c4, r9c5 or r9c6 -- all in box 8. That 4 is therefore box 8's 4 as well, which clears 4 from r8c5.

explanation.notation: Innies & outies over several houses: 2,5 in r1234567c9 => r23c9<>5, r6c9<>2
explanation.short: r2c9, r3c9 ≠ 5; r6c9 ≠ 2: rule of 45 -- the innie cells of column 9 total 26
explanation.teach: Column 9 must total 45. The cages lying completely inside add up to 7 = 7, so the uncovered cells r1c9, r2c9, r3c9, r4c9, r5c9, r6c9 and r7c9 must total 45 - 7 = 38 (r5c9 is already 4, r7c9 is already 8, leaving 26 for the rest). Treat r1c9, r2c9, r3c9, r4c9 and r6c9 as a virtual cage of 26: the only filling left is 1+3+6+7+9. No surviving combination uses 2 or 5 at all. Rule-of-45 sums turn any nearly-covered house into an extra cage.

Whichever one is right, box 9's 2 is on column 9, so the other cells of box 9 -- r8c8 and r9c8 -- can't be 2. This 'claiming' (box-line) pattern is worth checking whenever a line's candidates for a digit bunch up in one box.

explanation.notation: Alternating Inference Chain: 2,7,8 in r7c13,r7c14,r13c14,r16c13 => r16c13<>8
explanation.short: r16c13 ≠ 8: Alternating Inference Chain -- either r13c14 is 8 or r16c13 is 2
explanation.teach: Start from the idea that r13c14 is NOT 8: so r13c14 is 7 (it only holds 8 or 7), which stops r7c14 being 7, so r7c13 is 7 (the only other 7 in row 7), which means r7c13 isn't 2, so r16c13 is 2 (the only other 2 in column 13). So at least one end is true: r13c14 is 8 or r16c13 is 2. Each removed candidate clashes with both ends: r16c13 can't be 8 (it sees r13c14 and it is itself the 2 end). Build such chains from links you trust: two-candidate cells, digits with two spots in a house, and digits a cage or line must contain.
